title: Cap. XII: Blancus on ἁμαρτίαν — habit not bare past act; three rationes
pass_a_gloss: At last, says the learned man, that word ἁμαρτίαν in the Pauline place does not signify the habit of sin, or the habitual corruption which is in infants themselves also, but the act of sinning, and that a past one, by which nothing else can be understood except Adam's first sin. But this is to contradict Calvin and the other greatest men whom we follow, who explain that 'they sinned' of original vice. Yet he brings reasons. Because, I., he says, Paul speaks of the sin which entered the world, that is, into all men, through Adam, whom he calls one man. He assumes that original vice either is not sin, or did not enter into all men naturally begotten through that one man. II. because infants also are involved in this sin: for they are in the census of men, and of their number into whom death passed, and they do not die because of any other actual sin than an imputed one, because no other actual [sin] falls on them: but an imputed actual [sin] is nothing other than Adam's first sin. Infants indeed do not die because of any other actual sin than that first of Adam: but why do they not die proximately because of that habitual vice which makes all and every human being guilty of eternal death before God? This is what I have more than once observed: immediate imputation of Adam's first actual sin cannot be built up unless the guilt of the habitual vice is denied. III. he says, when Paul says in verse 17 that death reigned through one offense and in verse 19 that many were constituted sinners by one man's disobedience, those words 'one offense' and 'one man's disobedience' cannot look to anything but Adam's own deed, that is, the violation of the divine command. Be it so—what then? Does it follow that the word ἁμαρτίαν does not signify the habit of sin? or that Adam's first actual sin is imputed to us immediately, that is, before we are born corrupt? Death reigns through one offense so propagated according to habit into all that death reigns in all, because sin reigns. By one man's disobedience propagated and multiplied according to habit, many are constituted sinners. Why seek elsewhere the proximate cause of our death, when it betrays itself in us—in our body and members—inhering, namely that sin which, unless crucified by Christ's grace, reigns so mightily in us?
pass_b_english: At last the learned man says the Pauline word ἁμαρτίαν does not mean the habit of sin—the habitual corruption even in infants—but a past act of sinning, which can mean nothing but Adam's first sin. That contradicts Calvin and the other great men we follow, who take 'they sinned' of original vice. Still he offers reasons. I. Paul speaks of the sin that entered the world, that is all men, through Adam, called one man. So he assumes original vice is either not sin, or did not enter all naturally begotten through that one man. II. Infants too are wrapped in this sin: they count among those into whom death passed, and they die by no other actual sin than an imputed one, since no other actual sin befalls them; and that imputed actual sin is nothing but Adam's first. Yes, infants die by no other actual sin than Adam's first—but why not die proximately by that habitual vice which makes every human being liable to eternal death before God? As I have often said: you cannot build immediate imputation of Adam's first actual sin without denying the guilt of habitual vice. III. When Paul says in verse 17 that death reigned through one offense, and in verse 19 that many were made sinners by one man's disobedience, those phrases can look only to Adam's own deed—the breach of God's command. Grant it—what then? Does it follow that ἁμαρτίαν does not mean the habit of sin, or that Adam's first actual sin is imputed to us immediately, before we are born corrupt? Death reigns through one offense so far as it is propagated by habit into all, so that death reigns in all because sin reigns. By one man's disobedience propagated and multiplied by habit, many are constituted sinners. Why hunt elsewhere for the proximate cause of our death, when that inhering sin shows itself in our body and members—and unless Christ's grace crucifies it, reigns so mightily in us?
source_text: Tandem, ait vir doctus, vox illa ἁμαρτίαν in loco Paulino non significat habitum peccati, seu habitualem corruptionem, quae ipsis etiam infantibus inest, sed actum peccandi, eumque praeteritum, quo non potest intelligi aliud praeter primum Adami peccatum. Hoc vero est Calvino & aliis viris maximis, quos sequimur, contradicere, illud peccaverunt de vitio originali exponentibus. Affert tamen rationes. Quia I. inquit, loquitur Paulus de peccato quod introiit in mundum. i. in omnes homines, per Adamum, quem vocat unum hominem. Supponit vitium originale, aut non esse peccatum, aut non introiisse in omnes homines per unum illum hominem naturaliter procreatos. II. quia, hoc peccato involvuntur etiam infantes: sunt enim in censu hominum, & ex eorum numero, in quos mors transiit, nec moriuntur propter aliud peccatum actuale quam imputatum, quia aliud actuale in eos non cadit: actuale autem imputatum non est aliud praeter primum Adami peccatum. Non moriuntur quidem infantes propter aliud peccatum actuale quam primum illud Adami: sed cur non moriuntur proxime propter vitium illud habituale, quod omnes & singulos homines reos mortis aeternae coram Deo peragit? Hoc est quod jam non semel observavi, non posse imputationem immediatam primi Adae peccati actualis astrui, nisi negato habitualis vitii reatu. III. inquit, cum Paulus dicit vers. 17. mortem regnasse per unam offensam & vers. 19. multos esse constitutos peccatores unius hominis inobedientia; verba ista una offensa, & unius hominis inobedientia, non possunt aliud respicere quam ipsum factum Adami. i. divini mandati violationem. Esto, quid tum postea? Num inde sequitur, verbum ἁμαρτίαν non significare habitum peccati? aut primum Adami peccatum actuale nobis imputari immediate, seu prius quam nascamur corrupti? Mors regnat per unam offensam ita secundum habitum propagatam in omnes, ut in omnibus regnet mors, quia regnat peccatum. Unius hominis inobedientia secundum habitum propagata & multiplicata multi sunt constituti peccatores. Cur proximam mortis nostrae causam in alio quaerimus, cum se prodat ipsa in nobis, in corpore nostro, ac membris nostris, inhaerens, nempe illud peccatum, quod nisi crucifigatur gratia Christi, tam impotenter in nobis regnat?
